BOX 11.2  CLINICAL APPLICATIONS
Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) and Nutrient Interactions
Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is an intricate enzyme system
distributed predominantly in nervous tissue, liver, and lungs.
This enzyme system is responsible for inactivating the
neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin
once they have played their part in sending messages to the
brain. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) are drugs that
block this activity. When the excess neurotransmitters are 
not destroyed, they accumulate in the brain.
In addition to inactivating these neurotransmitters, MAO 
breaks down another amine called tyramine. When MAO is
blocked by an MAOI, levels of tyramine also rise. Excess
tyramine can cause sudden, sometimes fatal increases in
blood pressure. To avoid this life-threatening side effect,
those taking MAOIs must avoid or limit foods that contain
high levels of tyramine.
Tyramine occurs naturally in foods, but it is difﬁ cult to 
quantify the exact amount of tyramine in foods. Tyramine
can also vary among different brands of certain foods based 
on processing, storage, and preparation methods. It is also
formed from bacterial breakdown of protein in foods as 
they age.
MAOIs are most often prescribed for depression, bacterial
and protozoal infections, and Hodgkin’s disease.
